title: Exploring the Synergistic Potential of Quantum Annealing and Gate Model Computing for Portfolio Optimization
abstract_summary: This preprint extends the Large System Sampling Approximation (LSSA) hybrid approach by introducing a Maximum Independent Set (MIS)-based sampling method to form representative sub-systems that capture strongest asset correlations, enabling a combination of quantum annealing and gate-model VQE amplitude optimization for large-scale portfolio QUBO problems. The authors test the method on real Indian stock data (up to 64 assets), showing comparable performance to classical solvers while substantially reducing the number of sub-systems (samples) required.
methodology_description: The authors extend the Large System Sampling Approximation (LSSA) approach to portfolio optimization by introducing a coupling-aware sampling method based on a market graph and its Maximum Independent Set (MIS). From historical asset returns they compute expected returns (µ), covariance (Σ) and a correlation matrix which is thresholded (α) to create an asset graph. The MIS of this graph (formulated as a QUBO/Ising problem) provides representative 'placeholder' assets; for each MIS asset they form a sub-system consisting of the Ng most-correlated assets connected to that placeholder. Sub-systems (size Ng) are solved independently (quantum annealing or simulated annealing) to obtain sub-system ground states. The Ns sub-system solutions are combined as a weighted sum |Swc> = sum_i C(i) |GS_sub(i)>, where the amplitude coefficients C(i) are encoded on Ngb = ceil(log2 Ns) qubits and optimized using a VQE (shot-based local Qiskit simulator) to minimize the expectation value of the full-system Hamiltonian; the final global binary solution is approximated by sign(Swc). For larger N where solving the MIS directly would require N qubits, they apply LSSA recursively to the MIS problem (random sampling of smaller MIS sub-problems, recombination via VQE) (Level 2). Experiments use D-Wave Advantage_system4.1 (and simulated annealing) to solve sub-systems, PyQUBO to build QUBOs, and a local Qiskit simulator (2048 shots) for VQE amplitude optimization. Key hyper-parameters reported include sub-system sizes Ng (e.g., N/2 or N/4), maximum samples Ns (limited to N/2 in tests), correlation threshold α = 0.25 and risk-aversion γ = 0.5. Results are evaluated via an approximation ratio relative to exact (or D-Wave Tabu for larger N) and via return/volatility (efficient frontier) comparisons.
algorithms_used: Maximum Independent Set (MIS) via QUBO/Ising formulation
experimental_setup: Sub-systems solved on D-Wave Advantage_system4.1 (quantum annealer) and with simulated annealing. VQE amplitude optimization executed on a local shot-based Qiskit simulator using Ngb = ceil(log2 Ns) qubits with 2048 shots. Sub-system sizes Ng chosen as N/2 for N in {8,16,32,40,64} and Ng = N/4 for N in {40,64}. Number of samples Ns limited (max N/2). Correlation threshold α = 0.25. Risk-aversion γ = 0.5. Classical optimizer COBYLA used for VQE.
dataset_used: Real-world Indian stock market data (closing prices), 5 years of historical data, up to N = 64 assets. Expected returns and covariance/correlation matrices computed from the time series; used to create QUBO portfolio optimization instances.

experiment_input.size: Assets sets with N in {8, 16, 32, 40, 64}; time window: past 5 years
experiment_input.preprocessing: Compute expected returns vector µ and covariance matrix Σ from price history; compute correlation matrix and threshold at alpha (0.25) to build market graph; form sub-systems by selecting Ng most-correlated assets connected to each MIS placeholder asset; QUBO/Ising mapping applied (binary selection variables).

pipeline_steps: Compute µ, Σ and correlation matrix from historical price data
Threshold correlation matrix at α to create market graph G(V,E)
Formulate MIS as a QUBO and solve (directly or via LSSA random-sampling if N qubits unavailable) to extract MIS_assets
For each MIS asset, create a sub-system by selecting up to Ng most-correlated connected assets (sub-systems need not be mutually exclusive)
Solve each sub-system Hamiltonian (Ising/QUBO) using quantum annealing (D-Wave) or simulated annealing to get ground-state partial bitstrings
Aggregate Ns sub-system ground states as |Swc> = Σ_i C(i) |GS_sub(i)>
Encode coefficients C(i) into amplitudes on Ngb = ceil(log2 Ns) qubits and optimize them using VQE on a local Qiskit simulator (cost = <sign(Swc)|H|sign(Swc)>) with COBYLA optimizer and 2048 shots
Form final approximate full-system solution by taking sign(Swc) and evaluate

key_findings: [supported] The paper proposes an MIS (Maximum Independent Set)-based sampling method to create LSSA sub-systems that reduces the number of sub-systems (Ns) needed compared with random sampling LSSA.

[supported] In experiments on real Indian stock-market data up to 64 assets, the hybrid approach (annealer for sub-systems + VQE amplitude recombination on a gate-model simulator) produced solutions with approximation ratios comparable to a classical solver (D-Wave Tabu) for the tested instances.
[supported] Concrete empirical reductions in sample counts reported: for N=64, Ng=32, LSSA_random required Ns=32 while LSSA_MIS used Ns=12 and LSSA_MIS_random used Ns=13 (experimentally observed).
[supported] The method was implemented and tested using D-Wave Advantage_system4.1 for sub-systems and a local Qiskit shot-based simulator for the VQE amplitude optimization.

[supported] The MIS-selected assets are used as 'placeholder' representative assets and sub-systems are built from the most correlated assets to each placeholder, possibly overlapping across sub-systems to capture cross-group dependencies.

[supported] LSSA with MIS becomes equivalent to the original (random-sampling) LSSA in the low-correlation-threshold limit (i.e., when the market graph becomes dense), i.e., original LSSA is a special case of the proposed approach.
[supported] Experimental hyperparameters reported: risk-aversion γ = 0.5, correlation threshold α = 0.25, VQE used Ngb = ceil(log2 Ns) qubits and 2048 shots; classical optimizer COBYLA.

[speculative] The authors claim the MIS-based sampling 'intuitively' yields diverse representative assets and thus captures strongest couplings more effectively than random sampling in practical markets (this is an argument supported by limited experiments but presented as generally applicable).

[speculative] The paper suggests that alternate quantum methods (e.g., Grover Adaptive Search for sub-systems or variational non-orthogonal optimization to replace the VQE step) could further improve scalability and performance; this is presented as future work/theoretical possibility rather than demonstrated.

[speculative] The authors claim that hybrid annealer–gate quantum computing could become a valuable/practical tool for portfolio managers in the near future; this is a forward-looking, non-demonstrated claim.
results_summary: The authors extend LSSA by introducing MIS-based, correlation-aware sampling to form sub-systems for portfolio QUBO problems. They tested the approach on real Indian stock data up to 64 assets, solving sub-systems on a D-Wave annealer and using a local gate-model VQE simulator to recombine sub-system solutions. Empirically, the MIS-based sampling required substantially fewer sub-systems (e.g., Ns reduced from 32 to 12 for N=64, Ng=32) while achieving approximation ratios comparable to a classical Tabu solver in their experiments. The study reports implementation hyperparameters (γ=0.5, α=0.25, VQE shots=2048) and highlights that the method generalizes LSSA (random sampling is a special case at low threshold). The paper frames several speculative extensions (Grover, non-orthogonal variational methods) as future directions.

quantum_advantage_detail: The paper does not claim or demonstrate a clear quantum computational advantage over classical solvers. Instead, it demonstrates that a hybrid annealer + gate-model recombination approach can match (be 'at par with') the classical Tabu solver on tested instances up to 64 assets while reducing the number of LSSA samples. The authors present this as an empirical scalability/engineering improvement rather than a provable quantum speedup or advantage; broader claims about practical advantage are speculative/future-looking.
limitations: Current quantum hardware limits: large-scale portfolio problems cannot be solved directly on today's gate-based or annealing hardware (author-stated).
LSSA sampling cost: the number of sub-systems (Ns) required to capture quadratic interactions can grow combinatorially as Ng decreases, creating a delicate Ng vs Ns trade-off (author-stated).
Random sampling drawback: randomly selecting sub-systems can omit strong couplings and require many expensive calls to quantum hardware (author-stated).

MIS formulation qubit requirement: the MIS QUBO (used to select diverse assets) nominally requires N logical qubits, creating a scalability bottleneck unless the MIS itself is divided (author-stated).
Experimental scale: evaluation was limited to problems of up to 64 assets and specific Ng choices; results are therefore demonstrated only for modest problem sizes (author-stated).

Simplified problem model: the QUBO formulation used assumes binary long-only positions, equal budget per selected asset, static market conditions, and ignores transaction costs and other practical constraints (author-stated).

Use of simulators for amplitude estimation: the VQE amplitude optimization was performed on a local shot-based simulator rather than on real gate-based hardware, so hardware noise effects were not measured (author-stated).

Reliance on annealing for sub-systems in experiments: the implementation focused on quantum annealing for sub-systems; gate-based solvers for sub-systems were not empirically evaluated here (author-stated).
[inferred] Sensitivity to market-graph threshold: the method depends on a correlation threshold (α) to build the market graph; performance may be sensitive to this choice and requires tuning.
[inferred] Generalization across markets/data: results are shown for Indian market data; applicability and robustness across other markets, time periods, and asset universes are not demonstrated.

[inferred] Practical-constraint incorporation: the approach does not demonstrate handling of real-world portfolio constraints (cardinality, min/max weights, transaction costs, turnover limits, shorting), which could change formulation and performance.

[inferred] Cost and latency of quantum calls: while the method reduces number of samples relative to baseline, it still requires multiple annealer and VQE calls; the total classical/quantum runtime and resource cost are not quantified.
[inferred] Nooretical performance guarantees: the hybrid heuristic has no provable optimality or approximation bounds; performance is empirical and stochastic.

[inferred] Noise and device error robustness: because VQE was simulated and sub-systems were usually solved on an annealer, the approach's sensitivity to realistic device noise and embedding errors (chain breaks, calibration) is not characterized.

[inferred] Choice of Ng and Ns generality: the paper reports tuning choices (e.g., Ns ≤ N/2) that may not generalize; systematic guidance on selecting Ng, Ns for a given hardware/problem instance is not provided.

key_ideas: #idea:hybrid-approach — Combine quantum annealing (D-Wave) to solve correlated asset sub-systems formulated as QUBOs with a gate-model VQE that optimizes amplitude coefficients to recombine sub-system ground states, reducing overall qubit requirements.

#idea:hybrid-approach — Introduce a coupling-aware sampling method based on a market graph and its Maximum Independent Set (MIS) to form representative sub-systems that capture strongest asset correlations, substantially reducing the number of sub-systems (Ns) compared to random LSSA sampling.

#idea:near-term-feasibility — Demonstrated end-to-end on real Indian stock data (N up to 64) with approximation-ratio and efficient-frontier comparisons showing comparable performance to classical baselines while using fewer sub-systems.

#idea:hybrid-approach — Encode recombination amplitudes C(i) on Ngb = ceil(log2 Ns) qubits so the VQE recombination step scales logarithmically in Ns, enabling recombination of many sub-system solutions with few qubits.

#limitation:qubit-count — Direct MIS formulation would require N qubits for large N, forcing recursive LSSA (Level 2) to handle MIS extraction and indicating limitations in scaling due to available qubits.

#limitation:simulation-only — The VQE amplitude-optimization/recombination was executed on a local shot-based Qiskit simulator (2048 shots) rather than gate-model hardware, so the gate-model recombination step is not validated on real quantum processors.
